entries.title: Real testnet ledger in which SetOptions adds an ed25519 signed-payload signer

caps.note: Signed-payload signers exist since protocol 19 and are still rare on the network.

entries.shape: The first transaction is a SetOptions that adds a signer whose key is a signed payload (a P... strkey: a 32-byte ed25519 key plus a 3-byte payload). A signer key of this type is 40 bytes or more, so code that assumes every signer is a 32-byte account key truncates it, rejects it, or stops.

decoded.note: Equals the hash of the SetOptions transaction above, computed from its XDR and the network passphrase.

entries.title: Contract return value: a map whose keys u32 1 and symbol "1" print the same

caps.note: Soroban maps may hold keys of different types. The keys here are in host order (u32 before symbol).
TransactionMeta v4 first appears in the protocol 23 XDR.

source.notes: Decode-level entry: a minimal TransactionMeta v4 that carries only the return value. It is not the meta of a transaction that was applied.

entries.shape: The Soroban return value is a map with two entries whose keys are different values but convert to the same text, u32 1 and symbol "1". Code that turns the map into a string-keyed object keeps one entry and loses the other without an error.

entries.title: Contract call whose argument is a muxed contract address with an ID above 2^53

caps.note: This union case does not exist in the protocol 28 XDR, so a decoder built on older definitions must fail on this entry, not misread it.

source.notes: Decode-level entry: unsigned, with no Soroban resource data, so the network would not apply it. The source key is the ed25519 key of seed bytes 0..31; the contract IDs are SHA-256 of the labels shapecov:contract:a and shapecov:contract:b.

entries.shape: The second argument of the call is an ScAddress of the new muxed-contract type, with a 64-bit ID of 2^53 + 1. Software on pre-protocol-30 XDR cannot decode the address type, and software that holds the ID in a floating-point number reports 2^53.

entries.title: Offer ID, muxed IDs, memo ID and amount at 64-bit extremes

caps.note: Muxed source with ID 2^53+1 and muxed destination with ID 2^64-1.

source.notes: Decode-level entry: unsigned. No offer with this ID exists, so the network would apply the transaction with a failed result. No ledger in the scanned testnet range or in the stellar-core goldens carries an offer ID above 2^53, which is why this one is generated.

entries.shape: Every 64-bit identifier in the transaction is above 2^53: the offer ID and the source's muxed ID are 2^53+1, the destination's muxed ID and the memo ID are 2^64-1, and the payment amount is the largest signed 64-bit value. Held in a floating-point number, each becomes a different value.

offer_id.why: a number above 2^53 has already lost precision
empty; 0 means create a new offer

source.notes: Standalone network, manual close, fixed keys and close times; reproducible with tools/localcore_repro.py. See the scenario in tools/localcore.py.

entries.title: Local stellar-core, scenario participants-p28: a Soroban authorization entry declaring a contract deploy that never runs

source.notes: Standalone network, manual close, fixed keys and close times; see the scenario in tools/localcore.py.

entries.shape: The same transfer as localcore-planted-auth-5, carrying an unsigned address credential whose root invocation declares creating a contract from that address. No contract is created: the meta has no instance entry for it, and neither the declared deployer nor the contract appears anywhere in the meta. An indexer that records the declared deploy stores the creation of a contract that does not exist (stellar/wallet-backend 80121f3).

entries.title: Local stellar-core, scenario participants-p28: a Soroban authorization entry no require_auth matches, naming an account the ledger never touches

source.notes: Standalone network, manual close, fixed keys and close times; see the scenario in tools/localcore.py.

entries.shape: A caller transfers 1 XLM through the native Stellar Asset Contract and authorizes it with its own source-account entry. The operation carries one more authorization entry: an address credential for another account, declaring a transfer from it, with no signature. The host checks an entry only when a require_auth call matches it, so the transaction succeeds and that account appears only in the envelope: no ledger entry, nonce or event names it. An indexer that takes participants from the authorization tree records an account the transaction did not affect (stellar/wallet-backend 9538b3c).

entries.title: Local stellar-core, scenario failures-p30: 56 result codes no other entry has, set when a transaction fails at apply, in one ledger

source.notes: Standalone network, manual close, fixed keys and close times; see the scenario in tools/localcore.py.

entries.shape: About 60 transactions, each from its own account, each built so that one operation fails when stellar-core applies it against ledger state: account merge (sub-entries, sponsor, sequence too far, destination full), AllowTrust and SetTrustLineFlags failures, ChangeTrust (cannot delete, line missing, not authorized to maintain liabilities, low reserve), claimable balances, clawback, pool deposit and withdrawal, offers crossing themselves or hitting full lines, path payments without destination, trust or authorization, sponsorship revocations, SetOptions failures, an open sponsorship sandwich and a RETURN memo. Each code is set in an operation's doApply, never in its doCheckValid, so each can be in a closed ledger; run.json lists the code every transaction was built to produce.

entries.title: Local stellar-core, scenario failures-p30: the same apply-time failures inside fee bumps, so the inner transaction result carries them

source.notes: Standalone network, manual close, fixed keys and close times; see the scenario in tools/localcore.py.

entries.shape: As localcore-tx-failures-plain-12, with each victim wrapped in a fee bump paid by a third account: the outer result is txFEE_BUMP_INNER_FAILED and the inner result txBAD_SEQ, txBAD_AUTH, txBAD_AUTH_EXTRA (the attacker raised the master weight, so an extra signer's signature went unused), txBAD_MIN_SEQ_AGE_OR_GAP or txBAD_SPONSORSHIP, or an operation failing with opBAD_AUTH.

entries.title: Local stellar-core, scenario failures-p30: transactions that are in a closed ledger and failed the checks stellar-core repeats when it applies them

source.notes: Standalone network, manual close, fixed keys and close times; see the scenario in tools/localcore.py.

entries.shape: Each victim transaction was valid when it was queued. An attacker transaction of the same ledger, whose operation runs as the victim's account and is signed by it, changes the victim first: its sequence number (txBAD_SEQ), its master weight (txBAD_AUTH), a sequence-ledger gap (txBAD_MIN_SEQ_AGE_OR_GAP), or the signers of another operation's source (opBAD_AUTH). TransactionFrame::apply calls commonValid again, so the victim is in the ledger with that result. stellar-core orders transactions by hash, so each case is sent four times; some replicas apply before their attacker and succeed.

entries.title: Local stellar-core, scenario failures-p30: a ledger that applies base fee, base reserve, max transaction set size and ledger flags upgrades

source.notes: Standalone network, manual close, fixed keys and close times; see the scenario in tools/localcore.py.

entries.shape: Four network upgrades armed together and applied in one ledger: the upgrades list carries LEDGER_UPGRADE_BASE_FEE, BASE_RESERVE, MAX_TX_SET_SIZE and FLAGS, and from the flags upgrade on the ledger header carries the v1 extension with the flags. An indexer that reads fees or reserves from configuration rather than from the header gets every later ledger wrong.

entries.title: Local stellar-core, scenario big-merge-p30: a payment of 2^53 + 1 stroops and an account merge that moves more than 2^53

source.notes: Standalone network, manual close, fixed keys and close times; see the scenario in tools/localcore.py.

entries.shape: One transaction: the root account pays a new account 9,007,199,254,740,993 stroops (2^53 + 1), then that account, as its operation's source, merges into a third account, which receives 9,007,200,254,740,993. Both amounts are past the largest integer a float64 holds exactly, so a reader that parses stroops into a JavaScript number or a double stores them rounded; and the merge removes an account in a successful transaction.

entries.title: Local stellar-core, scenario trustline-churn-p28, first ledger: an account trusts USD

source.notes: Standalone network, manual close, fixed keys and close times; see the scenario in tools/localcore.py.

entries.shape: One transaction: a new account trusts USD issued by the root account. The first ledger of the sequence trustline-churn (corpus/sequences.json): an indexer that keeps current state writes the trustline row here.

entries.title: Local stellar-core, scenario trustline-churn-p28, second ledger: one transaction removes a trustline, adds it again and removes it again

source.notes: Standalone network, manual close, fixed keys and close times; see the scenario in tools/localcore.py.

entries.shape: One transaction of three CHANGE_TRUST operations on the trustline the previous ledger created: limit 0 (removed), a limit (created), limit 0 (removed). It ends removed, so an indexer replaying the sequence trustline-churn must hold no row for it; one that nets the create and the last remove to nothing keeps the row the previous ledger wrote (stellar/wallet-backend#687).
